title: Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897)
hookLine: she died at 24 in an obscure convent and became one of the most loved saints
last: SHE WAS ONLY ASKED TO TELL.

lines: A GIRL KNEELS BEFORE THE POPE.
cards: A girl of fourteen is in Rome with her father and a group of pilgrims, in line to meet the Pope. They've all been told firmly: do not speak to the Holy Father.

When her turn comes, she kneels, puts her hands on his knees, and asks him anyway. She wants to enter a convent now, at fifteen, not years later. He tells her, gently, that she will enter if God wills it.
The guards carry her away. A few months later she's inside the Carmelite convent in the small French town of Lisieux. She'll never leave it.
She'll die there at twenty-four, and almost nobody outside will have heard of her.

teach.h: TOO SMALL FOR THE GREAT SAINTS.
teach.b: Thérèse Martin grew up the youngest of five sisters in a devout family. Her mother died when she was four, and she was a sensitive, tearful child.
In the convent she read about the great saints, the martyrs and mystics, and felt tiny beside them. They were mountains; she was a grain of sand. So she went looking for a shortcut.
In her time, she wrote, the rich had lifts to save them climbing stairs, and she wanted a lift to God, because she was too small to climb the rough stairway of perfection.
She found it in a line of scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." The lift, she decided, was the arms of Jesus. She didn't have to become big.
She had to stay little and let herself be carried. That's the little way. In practice it looked ordinary.
She smiled at a sister who grated on her nerves, so sweetly that the sister thought she was her favorite. When another nun splashed her with dirty water in the laundry, she took it without complaint.
Small things, done with great love.
Dying of tuberculosis, she also went through a deep darkness, when heaven felt closed to her, and she kept going anyway.

teach.h: WHOSOEVER IS A LITTLE ONE, LET HIM COME TO ME.
teach.b: Her notebooks became a book, Story of a Soul, published a year after she died, and it spread around the world. She was canonized in 1925, and in 1997 named a Doctor of the Church, one of only a handful of women.

how: Catholics keep the feast of St. Thérèse on October 1, read her autobiography Story of a Soul, and many ask her prayers in novenas; she is a patron of the missions, though she never left her convent.

s: Thérèse traveled the world as a missionary
she entered the convent at fifteen and never left it. she died there at twenty-four.
she felt too small to climb to holiness like the great saints
so she looked for a lift instead of stairs, and found it in the arms of Jesus.
her faith was untroubled right to the end
in her last illness she went through a deep darkness, and kept going anyway.

games.q: you're Thérèse, fourteen, in line to meet the Pope. you've been told not to speak to him. what do you do?
o: ask him to let you enter the convent at fifteen.
give your request to a priest to pass on later.
games.why: she asked him anyway. he said she would enter if God willed it, and the guards carried her off. a few months later she was in the Carmel.

practice: Look ahead at your day and find its smallest, most forgettable task: washing a cup, answering a message, holding a door, listening to someone repeat a story.
Picture doing it slowly and warmly, as if it mattered, because Thérèse would say it does. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you do it.

wordCard.voice: Little Flower. Thérèse of Lisieux's own nickname, who found a small, hidden way to holiness anyone could walk.

carryVoice: Your line: the little way. Small, hidden, and open to anyone who wants it. Day ninety-three.
